t.3.49.1: When Rāvaṇa had been addressed thus, fittingly, by Jaṭāyus, all twenty of his eyes blazed like fire as he grew enraged.
t.3.49.2: His eyes reddened with anger, wearing earrings of refined gold, the impatient lord of the Rākṣasas rushed at the lord of birds.
t.3.49.3: In that great forest there arose a tumultuous clash between the two of them, like that of two wind-driven clouds in the sky.
t.3.49.4: Then there arose that wondrous battle between the vulture and the rākṣasa, like a clash between two great winged mountains wreathed in garlands.
t.3.49.5: Then the mighty one showered the king of vultures with nālīkas and nārācas, with sharp-pointed vikarṇis, most dreadful arrows.
t.3.49.6: In that battle the vulture Jaṭāyus, lord of birds, received upon himself those showers of arrows, the missiles of Rāvaṇa.
t.3.49.7: Then the mighty one, best of birds, with his two sharp-clawed feet inflicted many wounds upon his body.
t.3.49.8: Then, in his anger, Daśagrīva seized ten terrible arrows resembling the rod of Death, in his eagerness to crush his enemy.
t.3.49.9: He of great valour pierced the vulture with those arrows, loosed from a fully drawn bow and flying straight, with sharpened, keen and terrible shafts.
t.3.49.10: Seeing Jānakī, her eyes filled with tears, in the rākṣasa's chariot, he paid no heed to those arrows and rushed upon the rākṣasa.
t.3.49.11: Then the lord of birds, of great splendor, broke with his two feet his bow, together with its arrows, adorned with pearls and gems.
t.3.49.12: And with his wings the mighty lord of birds, of great splendour, shook apart Rāvaṇa's blazing quiver, which shone like fire.
t.3.49.13: In that battle the mighty one slew his swift, divine donkeys, which wore golden breastplates and had the faces of piśācas.
t.3.49.15: With his bow broken, his chariot gone, his horses slain and his charioteer killed, Rāvaṇa fell to the ground, holding Vaidehī in his lap.
t.3.49.14: He shattered the great chariot, that excellent car fitted with its triple pole, moving at its master's will, blazing like fire, its body adorned with jewels and gold. He broke as well the parasol that shone like the full moon, together with the fans.
t.3.49.16: Seeing Rāvaṇa fallen to the ground, his chariot shattered, all beings honored the king of vultures, crying, "Well done! Well done!"
t.3.49.17: But seeing that lord of the bird-flocks exhausted by old age, Rāvaṇa, delighted, seized Maithilī and flew up again.
t.3.49.18: As he went along, exultant, having placed Janaka's daughter on his lap, Jaṭāyu, the king of vultures, flew up and spoke these words to him.
t.3.49.19: O foolish Rāvaṇa, you are carrying off this wife of Rāma, whose arrows strike like the thunderbolt; surely it is for the destruction of the rākṣasas.
t.3.49.20: Together with your friends and kinsmen, together with your ministers, your army and your retinue, you are drinking this draught of poison as a thirsty man drinks water.
t.3.49.21: The undiscerning, who do not know the consequences of their deeds, perish very swiftly, just as you shall perish.
t.3.49.22: Bound by the noose of Time, where can you go that you will escape from it? You are like a fish that has seized the baited hook, only to meet its death.
t.3.49.23: O Rāvaṇa, the two invincible Kākutsthas, the Rāghavas, will never forgive your violation of this hermitage.
t.3.49.24: The deed you have done, coward that you are, is condemned by the world; this is the path trodden by thieves, not the one followed by heroes.
t.3.49.25: Fight, if you are a hero! Stand for a moment, Rāvaṇa, and you will lie slain on the ground just as your brother Khara did.
t.3.49.26: The deed that a man undertakes when his time of death has come, that very unrighteous deed you have undertaken, to your own destruction.
t.3.49.28: Having spoken these fitting words, the mighty Jaṭāyus fell violently upon the back of that rākṣasa, the ten-necked Rāvaṇa.
t.3.49.27: What man would ever do a deed whose consequence is sin, even if he were the lord of the worlds, the blessed self-born Svayambhū himself?
t.3.49.29: Seizing him with his sharp talons, he tore at him on every side, just as an elephant-rider would, mounted upon a vicious elephant.
t.3.49.31: Thus tormented again and again by the king of vultures, that rākṣasa, his lips quivering with rage, trembled violently.
t.3.49.30: Driving his beak into his back, he tore at him with his talons, and he whose weapons were his talons, wings and beak plucked out his hair.
t.3.49.32: Clasping Vaidehī tightly to his left side, Rāvaṇa, in pain and beside himself with rage, struck Jaṭāyu with the palm of his hand.
t.3.49.34: Then the mighty Daśagrīva, enraged, let go of Sītā and struck the king of vultures with both his fists and both his feet.
t.3.49.33: Then Jaṭāyu, the lord of birds and tamer of foes, overpowered him and with his beak tore off his ten left arms.
t.3.49.35: Then for a moment there took place a battle between those two of matchless valour, the chief of the rākṣasas and the foremost of birds.
t.3.49.36: Then Rāvaṇa, raising his sword, cut off both the wings, the feet and the flanks of him who was struggling for the sake of Rāma.
t.3.49.37: His wings suddenly severed by the rākṣasa of fearsome deeds, the vulture, struck down, fell to the earth with but little life remaining.
t.3.49.38: Seeing Jaṭāyuṣa fallen on the ground, drenched with blood, Vaidehī, grief-stricken, ran toward him as if toward her own kinsman.
t.3.49.40: Then Sītā, the daughter of Janaka, whose face shone like the moon, embraced once more that bird lying felled upon the ground, crushed by the violence of Rāvaṇa, and wept.
t.3.49.39: The lord of Laṅkā saw Jaṭāyus lying on the earth, he who looked like a dark rain-cloud, with a gleaming white breast and lofty valour, like a forest fire that had died down.
